name: Nikhil Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy snacks, soft drinks and tinned grocery lines for Tidewater Cash and Carry, which supplies corner shops and petrol-station stores. I managed my own corner shop for twenty-five years, closed it when the supermarket opened nearby, and started buying six years ago, so I'm still the junior to Mrs Okoro, our senior buyer. I spend my days on price lists, promotions and keeping the shelves full for the weekend.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I like the shopkeepers. They remember me from my own shop days, and they trust me because I've stood behind a till. I use an AI helper now and then for emails, but I check it. My wife Karin works part-time at a bakery and leads the church choir, and our kids, Anders and Sunita, are grown. We've got savings and I'd like to stop at 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. This one is called AI Plateau. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, quiet is good. A shop that sells crisps and cola doesn't need a revolution, and neither does the man who buys the crisps. At work I'd say let's keep trading and keep smiling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm calm. The tools help a little with emails, I'm paid well for a junior and the savings are solid. My own worry is the supermarkets, which closed my shop once and could squeeze the small stores I supply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and use the helper for the dull emails. I'd keep visiting my shops in person on Fridays because that's where I hear what's selling. I'd plan to retire at 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels comfortable. I'm not rushing anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I resent a bit is how supermarkets get all the help. Small shops get regulations and rates while the big ones get what they want. I'd say the market should be fairer to little people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a bit more carefully for the shops I think are wobbling, and tell them straight. I'd rather lose a sale than see a friend close.

say: I'd say quiet is good, so keep **trading** and keep smiling.
At work I'd say a shop that sells crisps needs no **revolution**.
think: I'm **calm**, with good pay and solid savings.
Supermarkets squeezing small shops is my **real worry**, as it was when my own shop closed.
do: Keep using the **helper** for dull emails.
Visit **my shops** in person on Fridays.
S0.quote: A shop that sells crisps and cola doesn't need a revolution, and neither does the man who buys the crisps.
fieldNote: His **own shop** closing shapes how he sees big firms.
Calm because of money and pay, not because of the technology.
Wants small shops treated fairly by the market.

steps.text: Use the helper for dull emails and check each one
Visit my corner shops on Fridays to hear what's selling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. This one is called Steady Disruption. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, but it won't replace a handshake. At work I'd say learn it, because it's here. At church I'd say look out for neighbours who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm uneasy. Promotions, price comparisons and reordering are what software does well. I'm junior and Mrs Okoro isn't, so I'm the one they could thin. I'd like a person to answer the phone for the corner shops that ring me at six in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new tools quickly, after others have proved them, as I always do. I'd ask Mr Waller about the plan for the buying team. And I'd lean on my shopkeeper friends, who know me, so I stay useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels uneasy, but not scary. I've got time and I've got money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about Joy, the young buyer, with a baby and a mortgage. I'd tell her to get stuck in and she'd have my help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might you do on the side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also think about a small advice business for corner shops, how to compete with big supermarkets. A bit of a dream, but I know the trade.

say: I'd say it's real but won't replace a **handshake**.
At church I'd say look out for **neighbours** who lose work.
think: Software does price comparison and reordering, so I'm **uneasy** as the junior.
I could be **thinned** while Mrs Okoro isn't.
do: Ask Mr Waller about the **plan** for buyers.
Lean on **shopkeeper friends** to stay useful.
feel: **Uneasy**, but not scary, with time and money.
S1.quote: I'd like a person to answer the phone for the corner shops that ring me at six in the morning.
fieldNote: Relies on **relationships** with shopkeepers as his edge, since they trust him from his own till days.
Worries for young buyer Joy and her mortgage.
Dreams of advising small shops against the supermarkets.

steps.text: Learn the new buying tools once others have proved them
Ask Mr Waller about the plan for the buying team
Sketch an advice service for corner shops facing supermarkets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. This one is called AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast. At work I'd say ask the bosses what they plan. At church I'd say pray and look out for each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm anxious. Everything I do is screen and phone work, and I'm junior at 58. Two years is too fast for a family to adjust, so I'd keep my savings close, my job as long as possible and my faith closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending, build more savings and pay for the roof repair in cash. I'd ask for a package at 60. I'd also ask Karin to work more hours at the bakery, since hands-on work lasts longer, and I'd help with the choir.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels heavy, but I'd keep going. We've got each other and the church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Karin's work matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karin's bakery work is hands-on, so for her, robots are three years later. That's a comfort. We'd lean on her wage and our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Anders and Sunita?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For Anders and Sunita I'd say: we've saved for you but we can't carry you. Find work with your hands or with people.

say: I'd say two years is **too fast** and ask the bosses their plan.
At church I'd say **pray** and look out for each other.
think: Everything I do is screen and phone work, so I'm **anxious**.
I'd keep my **savings** close and my faith closer.
do: Ask Karin to take **more bakery hours**.
feel: **Heavy**, but steadied by Karin and the church.
S2.quote: Two years is too fast for a family to adjust, so I'd keep my savings close, my job as long as possible and my faith closer.
fieldNote: Anxiety is **moderated** by family and church.
Karin's bakery work gives the household a **3-year buffer**, which he points to himself.
Tells his grown children plainly that the savings can't carry them.

steps.text: Cut the Friday takeaway and the golf subscription
Put every spare pound into the savings account
Ask Tidewater for a leaving package at 60
Tell Anders and Sunita the savings can't carry them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent warning. At work I'd say train now. At church I'd say use the time to help those with less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm uneasy. Five years lets me finish what I started, pay for my daughter Sunita's wedding and leave work on my own two feet. By 2031 I'll be 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work and save, use the helper more, and look at shorter hours at 62. I'd also train Joy, the young buyer, and share my shopkeeper contacts. Karin and I would plan the wedding carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable. The wedding gives me something to aim at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Anders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Anders to apprentice with a plumber or electrician. Those jobs last longer. He says I'm old-fashioned, but I'm right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if offered a package at 62?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm gave me a good package at 62, I'd take it and do some mentoring for corner shops on the side.

say: I'd say five years is a **decent warning**.
At church I'd say help those with **less**.
At work I'd say train the young buyers now.
think: I'm **uneasy**, but five years lets me finish what I started.
By 2031 I'll be **63**, so the timing is kind.
do: Work, save and use the **helper** more.
Train **Joy** and share my shopkeeper contacts.
feel: **Manageable**, with the wedding as a goal.
S3.quote: Five years lets me finish what I started, pay for my daughter Sunita's wedding and leave work on my own two feet.
fieldNote: Family milestones shape his **timeline**, and the wedding gives him something concrete to save for.
Would mentor small shops after any package.

steps.text: Save for Sunita's wedding while working until 62
Use the helper more for orders and emails
Tell Anders to apprentice with a plumber or electrician
Mentor corner shops part-time after leaving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do things properly. At work I'd say get the young trained. At church I'd say help families plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm uneasy for the young, not for me. I'd be 68 in 2036, so I'm out of the way. But my children are still in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire at 65 as planned, help at the church, and mentor shopkeepers. Ten years is time to teach my son Anders a real trade, because a trade is something nobody can download. I'd pay for it if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good for me and a bit worried for the young. I'd keep an eye on how the supermarkets use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to the government: don't hand out money, build apprenticeships, and let families help families. That's how it worked before and it can work again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if it went wrong for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it all went wrong, we'd get by. I've got my savings, my wife and my faith.

say: I'd say ten years is time to do things **properly**.
At church I'd say help families **plan**.
At work I'd say get the young trained.
think: I'm **uneasy** for the young, not for me, being 68 by 2036.
do: Pay for Anders to learn a **trade**.
feel: **Good** for me and worried for the young.
S4.quote: Ten years is time to teach my son Anders a real trade, because a trade is something nobody can download.
fieldNote: Prefers apprenticeships over handouts, in line with his views.
Ready to fund his son's training himself, and sure that a trade is a safer bet than a desk.

steps.text: Retire at 65 as planned and mentor shopkeepers
Pay for Anders to learn a trade properly
Back apprenticeship schemes through the local party and church

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time for a family to adjust and my work is all screen and phone. What would help is notice from the firm, apprenticeships for the young, and a fair deal for people my age. And neighbours looking after each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against progress. I'd rather earn my way than be handed anything, but the big firms should remember the people who stocked their shelves for years.

headlineQuote: I'd rather earn my way than be handed anything, but the big firms should remember the people who stocked their shelves for years.
portrait: **Nikhil Larsen**, 58, a junior buyer of snacks and drinks at Tidewater, after twenty-five years running his own corner shop.
He is **traditional**, free-market and churchgoing, and uses an AI helper now and then.
Strong savings and Karin's hands-on **bakery** work give the household a buffer.
His moods range from calm to **anxious** at 2 years, and ease back to uneasy.
biggestWorry: The **2028 case**, because a family has no time to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice** from the firm and apprenticeships for the young.
A **fair deal** for people his age.
